strengths: Provides a principled and well-motivated formulation of sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) for LLM-based interactive information gathering, with careful theoretical treatment of key design choices (prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation pairing, EIG estimation, belief updating).

Identifies and empirically demonstrates a subtle but important flaw in prior work: the implicit assumption of constant expected likelihood entropy reduces their 'EIG' to marginal predictive entropy, and shows this degrades performance (Section 3.2.1, Figure 1).

Introduces practical and well-justified innovations (Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimator, sample-then-filter belief updating pf(θ;ht), targeted candidate question generation) that are each ablated and motivated by clear reasoning about LLM failure modes (over-collapse, incompatibility with history).

Strong and comprehensive experimental results across two distinct tasks (20-Questions and active preference elicitation), multiple LLM backbones (Qwen, Mistral, GPT-4o/mini, Llama), and multiple datasets, showing large and consistent gains over reasonable baselines (e.g., 14%→91% success rate).

Includes robustness tests under model misspecification (different questioner/answerer LLMs) and an ablation directly comparing prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation pairings, supporting the paper's theoretical claims with evidence.
Extensive and thoughtful discussion of related work, clearly delineating how this method differs from and improves upon prior EIG-based and heuristic LLM questioning approaches.
weaknesses: All evaluations use LLM-simulated answerers and LLM-as-judge scoring rather than real human users, which may not fully capture the messier, less predictable response distributions of actual people, especially given the paper's own emphasis on likelihood misspecification.

No analysis of computational cost/overhead (number of LLM calls, latency) relative to baselines, which is an important practical consideration given the method requires candidate generation, hypothesis sampling, filtering, and EIG estimation at every turn.

Restriction to multiple-choice questions (to maintain tractable entropy estimates) limits the generality of the approach for more open-ended or free-form interactions, and this limitation is acknowledged but not empirically explored (e.g., only 2 baselines, no comparison to allowing free-text questions with alternative uncertainty proxies).

Direct quantitative comparison to closely related prior work (e.g., Kobalczyk et al., 2025) is not performed on equal footing due to lack of available code/results, relying instead on indirect arguments from the other paper's rebuttal statements, weakening the strength of the superiority claims relative to that specific baseline.

Some of the theoretical arguments in Section 4 (e.g., claims about which pairing better matches practical updating procedures) are presented as intuitive/qualitative reasoning rather than rigorously proven, and are only partially validated by a single ablation experiment.

The set of baselines is relatively narrow (Entropy and Naive QA); other plausible alternatives (e.g., self-consistency-based question selection, chain-of-thought prompting for question planning) are not compared.

strengths: Provides a principled and carefully reasoned theoretical framework for applying sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) to LLM-based information gathering, including a clear taxonomy of prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation pairings and when each is preferable.

Identifies and empirically demonstrates a specific, previously under-appreciated flaw in prior EIG-based LLM approaches (i.e., implicitly reducing EIG to predictive entropy by assuming constant expected likelihood entropy), supported by both a clear conceptual example (Figure 1) and strong empirical evidence (Entropy vs BED-LLM comparison).

Extensive experiments across multiple LLM families (Qwen, Mistral, GPT-4o/mini, Llama) and multiple tasks (20-questions across three domains, active preference elicitation), with consistent and often substantial gains over baselines.

Includes thoughtful robustness checks such as questioner/answerer model misspecification and a targeted ablation of the data-estimation alternative, which helps substantiate the paper's central design claims.

Clear discussion of practical engineering choices (sample-then-filter belief updating, candidate question generation strategies) with reasonable justification grounded in observed LLM behavior (e.g., over-collapse of pLLM(θ)).
weaknesses: All evaluation is performed with simulated LLM-based answerers rather than real human users, despite the paper's motivating applications (medical diagnosis, tutoring, surveys, personalization) being fundamentally human-facing; this significantly limits confidence in real-world applicability and generalization.

No analysis of computational cost/latency overhead of BED-LLM relative to baselines, despite the method requiring many additional LLM calls per turn (candidate generation, hypothesis sampling/filtering, and EIG estimation across M candidates and N hypotheses); this is an important practical consideration for an 'intelligent agent' framework that is entirely omitted.

The LLM-as-judge evaluation protocol for preference elicitation uses the same answerer LLM to both simulate the user and score recommendation quality against the same hidden persona, raising concerns about self-consistency bias inflating apparent performance gains.

Several key hyperparameters (rejection threshold for history-compatibility filtering, temperature T=1.3, N and M values) are chosen heuristically without systematic ablation or sensitivity analysis, limiting reproducibility and understanding of robustness.

The questions are restricted to multiple-choice/yes-no format throughout, which is a substantial simplification relative to the open-ended natural-language querying that most real applications (e.g., clarifying user intent, tutoring) would require; while acknowledged, this limits the generality of the claimed contribution.

The data-estimation ablation is only conducted on a single dataset/model combination (Celebrities, Qwen2.5-72B), which is insufficient to robustly support the paper's strong claims about the superiority of the prior-likelihood pairing across settings.

Theoretical discussion in Section 4 is largely qualitative/discursive rather than formally rigorous (no theorems or formal guarantees), reducing the strength of the 'principled' claims relative to what is empirically demonstrated.

Baseline comparisons omit any RL-finetuned or preference-optimized question-asking methods (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024, Wu et al. 2025, Mazzaccara et al. 2024 DPO variant) that are discussed in related work, despite these representing a natural and relevant comparison point for the claimed performance improvements.

strengths: Provides a principled, well-motivated formulation of adaptive LLM information gathering as sequential Bayesian experimental design, with careful theoretical treatment of the prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation joint model pairings and their respective trade-offs (Section 4 is particularly thorough).

Identifies and empirically demonstrates a concrete flaw in prior EIG-based LLM methods (the implicit assumption of constant expected likelihood entropy, reducing EIG to predictive entropy), and shows this degrades performance -- a genuine and non-obvious technical contribution.

Extensive and fairly convincing experiments across two distinct task types (20-Questions and active preference elicitation), multiple LLM backbones (Qwen, Mistral-Large, GPT-4o/mini, Llama-3.3), multiple datasets, and both matched and mismatched questioner/answerer settings, showing consistent and often large improvements over baselines.
Careful ablation isolating the effect of the prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation pairing, confirming the paper's theoretical claims empirically.

Good engineering contributions (sample-then-filter belief updating, Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimator, candidate question generation strategies) that are well justified and likely useful to practitioners.
Thorough related work discussion that clearly differentiates the approach from several concurrent/prior works and explains why those methods underperform.
weaknesses: All evaluation relies on simulated LLM answerers and LLM-as-judge scoring rather than real human users, which may not fully capture real-world response distributions or answer noise, limiting external validity of the claimed gains.

The method restricts questions to multiple-choice format to keep entropy estimation tractable; this is well-justified but still limits applicability to more open-ended or free-form information-gathering scenarios, and the paper does not demonstrate how the approach would extend to those cases.

Computational overhead of BED-LLM (candidate generation, hypothesis sampling/filtering, repeated EIG evaluation) relative to baselines is not clearly quantified, making it hard to assess practical cost-effectiveness versus Entropy or Naive QA.

The hypothesis-filtering/rejection mechanism (likelihood threshold for rejecting incompatible hypotheses, retention mechanism) involves several heuristic hyperparameters that are not deeply analyzed or ablated for sensitivity.

Dataset/sample sizes are relatively modest (100 targets per 20-Questions dataset, 200 simulated users for preference elicitation), and it is unclear whether results are averaged over multiple stochastic runs or just single trajectories per target, which affects the reliability of reported confidence intervals.

strengths: Provides a well-grounded and carefully reasoned theoretical framework for applying sequential Bayesian experimental design to LLMs, including a thoughtful analysis of the trade-offs between prior-likelihood and data-estimation joint model pairings (with clear practical guidance on when each is appropriate).

Introduces a Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimator that avoids the unrealistic deterministic-likelihood assumption made by prior works, and clearly demonstrates (both theoretically and empirically) why this assumption is problematic.

Extensive and well-designed ablation studies (Entropy, Data-Estimation, ICL Beliefs, Implicit Maximization) that isolate the contribution of each individual algorithmic component, strengthening the causal claims about what drives performance gains.

Strong empirical results across multiple LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B) and problem domains (20 Questions with three entity categories, and preference elicitation), showing large and consistent improvements over baselines.

Tests robustness to questioner-answerer model misspecification, which is an important and realistic consideration for real-world deployment where users' response distributions differ from the LLM's internal model.

Thorough appendix with additional theoretical discussion (e.g., connecting to the expected uncertainty reduction framework, choice of theta), prompts, and implementation details that aid reproducibility.
Clearly differentiates itself from and subsumes several existing approaches (Split-like methods) as special cases with more limited assumptions.
weaknesses: No discussion or reporting of the computational/inference cost overhead of BED-LLM (multiple candidate question generations, hypothesis sampling/filtering rounds, EIG estimation over N x M candidates) relative to baselines, which is important for practical adoption given the method requires substantially more LLM calls per turn.

All evaluation is simulation-based, using LLMs to play both questioner and answerer roles (or an LLM judge for preference elicitation); there is no human-subject evaluation, leaving open how well findings transfer to real, noisier, less consistent human responses.

Several hyperparameters (e.g., the 0.2 compatibility filtering threshold, number of hypotheses/questions sampled, temperature settings) appear heuristically chosen without systematic sensitivity analysis, raising questions about robustness to these choices.

The gains in the preference elicitation task are comparatively modest relative to the large gains in 20 Questions, and it is unclear how well the approach scales to even more open-ended or higher-dimensional target spaces.

The method is restricted to multiple-choice question formats to keep the likelihood entropy tractable, which somewhat limits generality and naturalness of the interactive dialogue compared to free-form question generation.

The guidance on choosing between prior-likelihood and data-estimation formulations based on relative complexity of theta and y spaces, while intuitively argued, remains largely heuristic/qualitative rather than rigorously justified or quantitatively validated beyond the two tested domains.

strengths: Provides a principled and carefully reasoned treatment of how to instantiate sequential Bayesian experimental design with LLMs, including an explicit discussion of the prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation factorization and when each is preferable depending on the relative complexity of theta and y spaces.

Identifies and corrects a specific, previously under-examined flaw in prior information-theoretic question-selection work: the implicit assumption of a deterministic likelihood, which collapses EIG to marginal predictive entropy; the paper provides both a clear illustrative example and empirical evidence (Entropy ablation) that this matters.

Extensive ablation study (Entropy, Data-Estimation, ICL Beliefs, Implicit Maximization) that cleanly isolates the contribution of each individual design decision (objective, model pairing, belief updating, explicit vs. implicit optimization), which strengthens the causal claims about what drives performance.

Strong and consistent empirical gains across 5 different LLMs, 3 datasets in 20 Questions, and a separate preference-elicitation task, including robustness checks under questioner-answerer model mismatch, which support generalizability of the approach.

Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimator is theoretically justified (lower variance than sample-based alternatives used in prior work) and the paper is explicit and self-aware about approximations and their limitations throughout (e.g., §A, §B discussions).

Good positioning relative to related work, explicitly explaining how several prior methods (Piriyakulkij et al., Hu et al., Kobalczyk et al., Cooper et al.) reduce to special cases of the paper's Split/Entropy baselines.
weaknesses: No compute-matched comparison: BED-LLM requires substantially more LLM calls per turn (candidate question generation, hypothesis sampling/filtering, and EIG estimation over M candidates and N hypotheses) than the Naive baseline (single generation), yet the comparisons are framed purely in terms of success rate without discussing cost-accuracy tradeoffs or whether a compute-matched Naive/Split variant (e.g., more samples, self-consistency) would narrow the gap.

All evaluation is simulated: both the 'user' (answerer) and the quality judge (LLM-as-judge for preference elicitation) are themselves LLMs, with no human-subject evaluation; this raises concerns about whether gains measured in this closed-loop LLM-vs-LLM setting transfer to real interactive use with human users, whose answer distributions may differ qualitatively from a prompted LLM-answerer.

Several core components rely on heuristic, manually-tuned choices (e.g., compatibility-filtering threshold of 0.2, fixed temperatures, number of regeneration rounds, uniform-distribution assumption over filtered hypotheses rather than importance-reweighting) without sensitivity analysis showing robustness to these hyperparameters.

The method restricts candidate questions to multiple-choice format to keep likelihood estimation tractable, which limits applicability to more open-ended, free-form interactive settings that motivate the paper (e.g., general tool use, clarifying free-text intents) and is not evaluated outside this constrained setting.

The 'Split' and 'Entropy' baselines, while useful ablations, are essentially internal special cases of the authors' own framework rather than faithful re-implementations of the actual external methods cited (Hu et al., Kobalczyk et al., Piriyakulkij et al., Cooper et al.); the claim that these baselines are stronger than prior published numbers is asserted but not rigorously validated against the original implementations/settings.

Success-rate evaluation in 20 Questions relies on exact string matching to a fixed target list, which, despite some manual curation of alternative names, may still misjudge correct-but-differently-phrased guesses, introducing noise into the primary metric.

The paper's theoretical framing emphasizes principled Bayesian design, yet the actual implementation deviates substantially from exact Bayesian updating (rejection filtering, hypothesis retention heuristics, uniform re-weighting), and the gap between the theoretical narrative and the engineered heuristic implementation is not quantitatively characterized.

strengths: Provides a principled, well-motivated formulation of sequential Bayesian experimental design for LLM-based information gathering, with a clear and careful theoretical treatment of the key design choices (prior-likelihood vs data-estimation pairing, belief updating, EIG estimation).

Identifies and empirically demonstrates a specific flaw in prior work (the deterministic-likelihood assumption that collapses EIG to marginal predictive entropy), and shows this flaw matters empirically via the 'Entropy'/'Split' ablations.

Strong empirical results: large, consistent improvements over Naive and Split baselines across multiple LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B) and multiple problem categories (Animals, Celebrities, Things), including notably large gains for smaller models.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each algorithmic component (EIG vs entropy objective, prior-likelihood vs data-estimation pairing, filtered vs naive in-context belief updates, explicit vs implicit EIG maximization), which convincingly support the paper's design claims.
Tests robustness to questioner-answerer model mismatch, which is important for real-world deployment and strengthens the practical relevance of the method.

Extends evaluation beyond the closed, small-hypothesis-space setting common in prior work (no explicit restriction on the space of θ), and additionally evaluates on a more open-ended preference elicitation task with LLM-as-judge scoring, showing the approach generalizes beyond yes/no games.

Extensive appendix with thoughtful theoretical discussion (e.g., alignment between EIG formulation and belief-updating procedure, choice of θ, alternative framings) that adds rigor and clarifies when each design choice is appropriate.
Reasonably good positioning relative to related work, explicitly explaining why previous EIG-based LLM querying methods are special cases/ablations of the proposed framework.
weaknesses: No analysis of computational cost/latency: BED-LLM requires many additional LLM calls per turn (candidate question generation, hypothesis sampling, filtering, likelihood evaluations), but efficiency trade-offs versus baselines are not quantified, which matters for practical deployment.

Evaluation relies heavily on LLM-generated ground truth (e.g., synthetic user profiles generated by an oracle LLM) and LLM-as-judge scoring for preference elicitation, with no human evaluation to validate that these automatic metrics track real user satisfaction.

The construction of pf(θ; h_t) (uniform distribution over filtered/sampled hypotheses, fixed compatibility threshold of 0.2) is a heuristic whose sensitivity to hyperparameters (threshold, number of samples, temperature) is not systematically studied, despite the paper's own analysis showing belief construction is critical to performance.

Only two task families are studied (20 Questions-style guessing and single-domain movie preference elicitation); broader validation on other interactive settings mentioned in the introduction (tool use, clarification, troubleshooting) is absent, limiting evidence for the claimed general-purpose applicability.

No comparison against policy-based/amortized BED approaches (mentioned in related work as complementary) even in a simplified form, so it's unclear how much of the myopic EIG approach's gains would hold up against non-myopic alternatives.

The termination/guessing mechanism and prompt engineering details (e.g., diversity-encouraging prompts, reordering of context) involve many manually tuned choices whose individual necessity is not ablated, raising some reproducibility and generalizability concerns.
